materials.name: Cob

period.text: About 1300: the earliest standing cob buildings in the isles (exceptional survivals); popular in Devon up to the 19th century, when vernacular building generally ceased; revived since the 1990s (a new cob house in England in 1994 was reputedly the first in 70 years, and one in County Cork in 2002-04 the first in Ireland for about a century)

regions.text: Devon and Cornwall above all; also Anglesey, Cumbria, the East Midlands, Hampshire, Donegal Bay and Munster; chalk cob (wychert) in Buckinghamshire

materials.technology: Subsoil dug on the site, mixed with straw and water (traditionally trodden by oxen) and laid in courses on a stone plinth, each course left to dry; railways and mass-produced brick and slate ended vernacular building in the 19th century.
materials.note: The word cob is attested only from about 1600. Earth walling of the same kind is called mudwall in Scotland and clay dabbins in Cumbria (see mud-walling); wychert of Buckinghamshire is a chalk cob.

materials.name: Clay lump

period.text: Late 18th century (taken as about 1775): the earliest clay lump house the Norfolk Historic Environment Record names (Green Farmhouse, Toftwood, cased in brick about 1800); many early 19th-century examples; the latest named here is the steam-engine repair shop at Harling, built in the 1890s, possibly the largest clay lump building in Britain

materials.name: Mud and clay walling (clay dabbins, mudwall, Irish mud houses)

period.text: 1462: the earliest tree-ring date of the clay dabbins of the Solway Plain (dates run 1462-1788; many dabbins are of the 17th century); clay walls were used in medieval Scotland and earth was once the main material there; declined with the Industrial Revolution; Irish mud houses were built into the 19th century and lived in until the late 20th; repairs in the old way continue

regions.text: The Solway Plain of north Cumbria (the only substantial survival of a tradition once common in northern England and southern Scotland); south-west Scotland, Dundee and the Carse of Gowrie, Moray (clay and bool); Lincolnshire and Lancashire (mud and stud); much of rural Ireland (Limerick, Clare, Wexford)

materials.technology: Clay mixed with straw laid in thin lifts, each separated by a layer of straw, on the Solway; earth walls carry little load, so they were often combined with cruck roofs.

materials.name: Earthfast posts (post-hole construction)

period.text: 4000-3400 BC: the Neolithic timber hall at Balbridie, Aberdeenshire, known from its large post-holes, among the earliest timber houses in Europe; the usual way of building in timber until framing on sills, padstones or low walls became ubiquitous from about AD 1200; earthfast posts are still used for impermanent buildings

materials.technology: Posts set in the ground rot at the foot, so buildings were short-lived; raising the frame on a sill beam, padstones or a low wall kept the timber dry and made houses longer-lived.

materials.name: Timber framing

period.text: About 1200: framed buildings raised off the ground replaced earthfast posts from around AD 1200, and surviving timber-framed buildings in England go back to the 13th century; the most common structural material in most of England until brick superseded it (from the 15th-16th centuries in the south-east; vernacular building ceased in the 19th century); half-timbering revived after 1860 and green-oak framing since about 1980

regions.text: Most of lowland England, especially East Anglia, the Weald, Warwickshire, Worcestershire, Herefordshire, Shropshire and Cheshire; the Welsh March; almost absent from Cumbria

materials.technology: Abundant oak; the frame was filled with wattle and daub, later brick; cheap brick, the rebuilding laws after the Great Fire of London (brick and stone preferred) and the railways ended it as ordinary building.

materials.name: Cruck framing

period.text: 1262: the earliest surviving cruck, at the Royal George, Cottingham, Northamptonshire (tree-ring dated); documents name crucks ('forks') from 1189 in Somerset; more than three quarters of dated crucks were built in the 15th and 16th centuries; the latest dated ones are 1742 in England and Wales, 1690 in Ireland and 1801 in Scotland; crucks have been built again in green-oak framing since about 1980

regions.text: Wales, the Welsh March, the West Midlands, Devon and the north of England, with Scotland and Ireland; entirely absent from a swathe of eastern England from Kent and Sussex through East Anglia and Lincolnshire to the Humber. Jointed crucks belong to east Devon, west Dorset and Somerset; raised crucks set on walls are found in Scotland

materials.technology: Needs large curved oaks of a kind found at woodland edges; one explanation for the absence of crucks in the east is that coppiced woodland there gave straight timbers suited to box frames instead. Crucks went out of use when two full storeys were wanted.

examples.name: The Royal George, Cottingham, Northamptonshire
examples.note: earliest surviving tree-ring-dated cruck

examples.name: Leigh Court Barn, Worcestershire

materials.note: Origins are disputed: older writers saw crucks as prehistoric or 'early Celtic'; N. W. Alcock rejects that for want of evidence before the 13th century and thinks an 11th-century origin plausible, near the Welsh March and West Midlands. Why crucks are absent from the east is also argued: separate western and eastern carpentry traditions, or (P. Barnwell) coppice management that gave no suitable trees. Variants (FISH): base cruck, raised cruck, middle cruck, upper cruck, jointed cruck, end cruck.
